Þór, fully clothed in a wool tunic and cloak, raises the short-handled Mjölnir over two spread goat skins. Two billy goats rise from the skins; one clearly favours a hind leg. The farmer, his wife, boy Þjálfi and girl Röskva shrink together near the wall, terrified; Loki watches. No gore, exposed body or fire (omitted in this graded retelling), no lettering. This is afi’s telling, not the Hamrar household; keep myth woodcut distinct from farm watercolour.

cover.alt: The priest tests the children’s reading during his house visitation at Hamrar. Ásta reads confidently; Siggi waits for his turn.
cover.art_brief: Late November 1874, baðstofa at Hamrar in Jökuldalur. Ink and watercolour, established character bible. Séra Þorvaldur sits at a small wooden table with an open parish register, a pen and the lit household fish-oil lamp. Fully clothed children stand in a short row: six-year-old Ásta in her new skotthúfa reads the small catechism confidently; eleven-year-old Siggi waits next, red-faced and tense. Guðrún and Bjarni watch in clean woollen farm clothes. Low turf-house interior, beds along walls, no modern furniture. Keep lettering on pages illegible; no captions.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Helga les sögu. Ásta les kverið, en Óli segir: „Hún kann kverið!“
Afi segir: „Fólkið les grös á heiðinni. Eitt og eitt.“
Afi og Siggi lesa stafi, einn og einn. Svo eru þeir orð. „Ég les grös!“ segir Siggi.
Um morguninn les Siggi hægt, en vel.
words_with_history.note_en: Lesa can mean gathering or picking as well as reading. Afi uses the gathering sense in lesa grös: picking useful plants or Iceland moss on the heath. Siggi carries the image across to gathering letters into words. The precise local naturalness of lesa grös remains a review question.

Learner-load ledger: 29 new lexemes (28 single items including the title séra, and one chunk á morgun; includes is-skinn in the 30 ceiling); fermist ekki is a supported formula, not a thirtieth lexeme. Productive G08 forms include les/lest/lesum/lesið/lesa; fer/ferð/förum/fara; kem/kemur/koma; tek/tekur; sef/sefur/sofa; segi/segir; sé/sér/sérðu; brýt/brýtur; þekki/þekkir, reynir and lærir. Vil/get/veit/kann and formal þér with 2pl verb, imperatives and sérðu remain supported items, never drilled or tabled.

Local first-use clusters: s001–s026 visitation, catechism, reading/test/ability and judgment; s050–s063 ability and learning alongside the gathering metaphor; s081 ordinary hammer; s094–s104 strength, goats, wagon, hides, bones and breaking; s118 sea/fishing/serpent; s123 page. Every new item has an aid at or before its actual first encounter. Suggested briefing segment numbers were checked against the actual 126 segments. The boat SVG carries three labels within one diagram rather than three margin glosses.

Seven authored SVGs are specifically requested or useful for concrete first-use support, exceeding the generic two-diagram advisory. Goat/wagon and skin/bones diagrams preview related items together; planned rasters never carry support. Four rasters remain planned: cover, myth scene, kver and Mjölnir vignettes. Visual inspections are recorded after rendering.

Grammar explanation intentionally exceeds the short-note advisory: terms, formation, attested cells, translated examples and supported-versus-productive boundaries require space. Weak -ir includes þekkja/þekki; the new veiða is weak -ir too. Present-singular i-umlaut is distinguished from plural u-umlaut (fara/förum), and brjóta/brýt is its own vowel alternation.

Source: Snorra-Edda, Gylfaginning 21, 44 (first half), and one anticipatory sea-serpent line from 48; Netútgáfan numbering, https://netutgafan.snerpa.is/snorri/gylf.htm; treatment retold by afi, not quotation. Simplifications: Þór takes the goats and the household eats them (drepa waits until Kafli 17). Þór er ekki glaður replaces anger (reiður waits until Kafli 13). Fire is omitted. Taktu bæinn! Source spelling Mjöllnir is normalized as the course’s Mjölnir. The next myth journey waits for Kafli 24.

grammar.title: ég fer · við förum · ég les
grammar.rule: Ég les hægt. · Þú lest hægt. · Við lesum saman. · Nú fer ég.
grammar.note_en:
A verb says what someone does or what happens. The subject is the person or thing doing it. First person is the speaker: ég, “I”, and við, “we”; second person is the addressee: þú, “you”, one person, and þið, “you”, more than one; third person is someone or something spoken about: hann, “he”, or þau, “they”. Singular means one, plural more than one. The present is the form used here for what happens or is true now. The infinitive is the dictionary form, such as lesa, “read”. The tables show only forms actually encountered in the story. Empty cells mean “not met in this chapter”, not “no form exists”. A third-person cell is the same whether its subject is a pronoun or a name. In the headers, nf. abbreviates nefnifall, the nominative case used for the subjects here; nútíð means present and nafnháttur means infinitive.

Lesa is a strong verb, a class whose forms cannot all be built by adding the regular -ar endings. Its present singular keeps the vowel e: ég les, “I read”; þú lest, “you read”; hann les, “he reads”. Ég les illa (s050) means “I read badly”; Þú lest hægt (s051), “You read slowly”; Hann les hægt, en hann les vel (s072), “He reads slowly, but he reads well”. The first- and third-person singular are identical, les; only þú has the extra -t. For the plural, remove infinitive -a and add -um for við or -ið for þið: við lesum, “we read”, and þið lesið, “you all read”. Third-person plural uses lesa: börnin lesa (s001), “the children read”. Við lesum saman (s063) means “We read together”; Þið lesið vel á Hömrum (s087), “You all read well at Hamrar”. This ordinary þið addresses the household, in contrast to formal þér below.

Some strong verbs change the vowel in the present singular. This is called i-umlaut, a historical vowel change; the old sound that caused it is no longer visible in these forms. Fara → fer, “go → I go”, taka → tek, “take → I take”, and koma → kem, “come → I come”, show a → e or o → e; sofa → sef, “sleep → I sleep”, shows o → e too. The labelled diagram at s068 compares these three patterns: fara → ég fer, koma → ég kem, taka → ég tek.

It is not a rule that every a or o in every verb changes. Learn which verbs belong to this pattern. For fara, the first- and third-person singular are fer; þú adds -ð: ferð. Ég fer heim á morgun (s033) means “I go home tomorrow”; Hvert ferð þú, Siggi? (s047), “Where are you going, Siggi?” The plural uses the other stem: við förum, “we go”; þau fara, “they go”. Við förum út með séra Þorvaldi (s080) means “We go outside with Reverend Þorvaldur”; þau fara með honum (s113), “they go with him”. The a → ö in förum is u-umlaut before -um, a different change from the singular i-umlaut. The chapter has no ordinary þið form of fara to tabulate; its encountered farið belongs to the supported formal expression below.

Ég kem (s068) means “I am coming”; Séra Þorvaldur kemur (s004), “Reverend Þorvaldur is coming”. Ég tek strákinn og stelpuna (s112) means “I take the boy and the girl”; Presturinn tekur bókina (s025), “The priest takes the book”. Ég sef ekki (s048) means “I am not sleeping”; hann sefur ekki (s045), “he is not sleeping”. Compare the singular pairs kem/kemur, tek/tekur and sef/sefur: the first person has no -ur, and the third person adds -ur. These are the cells encountered here; do not extend the table to unseen persons. Brjóta has the related singular change jó → ý: ég brýt, “I break”, and hann brýtur, “he breaks”. Ég brýt ekki bein (s115) means “I do not break bones”; strákurinn tekur bein og brýtur það (s104), “the boy takes a bone and breaks it”.

Segja, “say”, is a -ja verb. In the met singular forms the final infinitive -ja becomes -i for ég and -ir for þú or hann: segi, segir. Nú segi ég ekki orðið (s060) means “Now I do not say the word”; Þú segir það (the same segment), “You say it”; segir Siggi (s019), “Siggi says”. The ending depends on the subject even when the verb comes before that subject. These examples illustrate the encountered word order; general inversion is not a drill here.

Þekkja, “know, recognise”, has ég þekki, “I know”, and þú þekkir, “you know”: remove -ja and use -i or -ir. Ég þekki Hall (s043) means “I know Hallur”; Þekkir þú Hall? (s040), “Do you know Hallur?” Hall is the accusative, or object form, of the name Hallur. This is a weak -ir pattern, distinct from the strong patterns above. The met weak forms þú lærir (s063), “you learn”, and hann reynir (s061), “he tries”, likewise have -ir. The examples do not supply the other persons of these two verbs, so those cells stay empty. Form work asks only for cells already read, never for an unseen paradigm.

Several expressions are supported items to recognise now, not systems to drill or tabulate. Viljið þér kaffi? (s010) means “Would you like coffee?” Þér is a formal “you” addressed here to one person, the priest. It takes a second-person plural verb: Viljið þér, “would you like”; prófið þér Sigga aftur? (s034), “will you test Siggi again?”; Þekkið þér Hall? (s041), “Do you know Hallur?”; Farið þér heim? (s079), “Are you going home?”; Þér þekkið Eddu (s085), “You know the Edda”. These are bounded formal expressions. They do not mean that several priests are present. Ordinary þið in s087 addresses several household members. The contrast is explained here, without gaps or a formal-address paradigm.

Ég vil (s112), “I want”; hann vill (s104), “he wants”; ég get það ekki (s050), “I cannot do it”; ég veit það ekki (s024), “I do not know that”; ég kann stafina (s019), “I know the letters”; þú kannt að lesa (s015), “you know how to read”; and hún kann kverið (s016), “she knows the catechism by heart”, are learned as items now and as a system later. Vil plus an infinitive expresses wanting to do something: ég vil lesa (s124), “I want to read”. Kann að plus an infinitive expresses knowing how: kannt að lesa, “know how to read”. Kann kverið has no að and means knowing the text by heart, the point of Óli’s joke. Veit concerns a fact; þekki concerns familiarity with a person or book.

Komdu, Ásta (s013), “Come, Ásta”; Komið, börn (s080), “Come, children”; and Taktu bæinn! Taktu féð! (s111), “Take the farm! Take the livestock!”, are supported commands. A command is called an imperative. Learn these whole expressions without producing other imperative forms. Sérðu in Hvað sérðu? (s052), “What do you see?”, is the joined form sérð þú; it is shown, not drilled. Ég sé stafi (s053) means “I see letters”. Hann fermist ekki (s026) means “He will not be confirmed”: fermist is a church formula here, with its verb system postponed. It states the reading requirement; it does not establish Siggi’s confirmation age or date.

Lesa also has the older sense “gather, pick”. Um sumarið les fólkið grös á heiðinni (s054) means “In summer the people gather herbs/lichen on the heath”. Grös is the plural of gras, here the plants gathered rather than a lawn. Siggi’s Ég les grös! (s058), “I gather herbs!”, carries afi’s image into his gathering of letters into words. This sense does not alter the present forms of lesa.
